issues.legal_issue: A state agrarian-reform law concerning village common lands may govern those lands even where an evacuee’s interest in them had vested in a central custodian.
material_facts: Village common lands were held for common village use by proprietors in proportion to their interests in other village lands.
The interest of proprietors who migrated was limited to their interest in the common lands and vested in the custodian under central evacuee-property legislation.
The state law vested rights, title, and interest in village common lands in the village panchayat as part of an agrarian-reform measure.
issues.conclusion: The state law prevailed in respect of the village common lands. Although the Court identified a direct conflict between the provisions on vesting and held that the presidential assent did not resolve that conflict, it adopted the view that the state law was, in pith and substance, a law concerning land and agrarian reform within the State Legislature’s competence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered Article 246(3) and Entry 18 of the State List, concerning land and rights in or over land, alongside Entry 41 of the Concurrent List, concerning custody, management, and disposal of evacuee property, and Article 254. It adopted the reasoning that a law concerning agrarian reform and village common lands could operate in the State’s own legislative field even though it affected property vested in the custodian. Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab was relied on for the characterization of the common-lands legislation as agrarian reform and its protection under Article 31-A.

predicates.state_law_concerns_agrarian_reform: The state legislature enacted a measure directed to agrarian reform and village welfare.
predicates.state_law_regulates_village_common_land: The state law governs rights in land reserved for common village purposes.
predicates.evacuee_vesting_preserves_the_former_own: The central custodian received the evacuee’s existing interest in the land rather than a different or enlarged interest.

issues.definition: When a state law is an agrarian-reform measure governing village common land and central vesting preserves only the former owner’s interest, the state law governs that land.

issues.legal_issue: Presidential assent sought for a specific constitutional purpose does not give a state law priority over an inconsistent earlier central law for a different purpose.
material_facts: The state law was reserved for presidential assent to obtain constitutional protection for a measure of agrarian reform.
The assent was sought for that specific purpose, not because the state law conflicted with the earlier central law governing evacuee property.
The President was not apprised that assent was sought to resolve that conflict.
issues.conclusion: The assent could not be used to give the state law priority over the earlier central law on the question of vesting evacuee property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 254(2), presidential assent may allow a state law on a Concurrent List matter to prevail over an inconsistent earlier central law. The Court held that assent sought and given for a specific purpose has efficacy limited to that purpose; assent obtained for the purpose of Article 31-A did not automatically amount to assent under Article 254(2) for resolving a different repugnancy. Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab was cited in connection with the agrarian-reform character of the state law.

predicates.state_law_conflicts_with_earlier_central: The state law contains a provision inconsistent with an earlier central law on the same matter.
predicates.presidential_assent_sought_for_different: The state government sought presidential assent to the law for a specific purpose other than resolving the inconsistency with the earlier central law.
predicates.president_not_informed_of_conflict: The President was not informed that assent was sought because the state law conflicted with the earlier central law.

issues.definition: If assent was sought for a different specific purpose and the President was not informed of the conflict, the assent does not give the state law priority for that conflict.

issues.legal_issue: Vesting an evacuee’s interest in village common land in a custodian does not enlarge that interest or permit the custodian to allot the land for separate or exclusive use.
material_facts: The common lands were indivisible, inalienable, and reserved for common village use.
A proprietor’s interest in the common lands was limited and did not pass merely through an alienation of the proprietor’s other land.
The custodian received the interest held by the migrating proprietor, subject to the same limitations.
issues.conclusion: The custodian could not free the evacuee’s interest from its limitations or allot the common lands for the separate or exclusive use of displaced persons.
issues.legal_principle: The custodian takes an evacuee’s property interest as it existed, quantitatively and qualitatively, subject to its existing incidents and limitations. The Court relied on the established characteristics of village common lands and referred to Rahman v. Sai and Rattigan’s Digest of Customary Law in the Punjab for the nature and limitations of interests in such lands.

predicates.land_is_reserved_for_common_village_use: The land is held for the shared use of the village community.
predicates.evacuee_interest_is_indivisible_and_nont: The migrating owner’s interest in the common land cannot be divided or alienated for separate use.
predicates.custodian_receives_only_existing_interes: The custodian receives the interest that the migrating owner held, subject to its existing limitations.

issues.definition: When land is reserved for common village use and the custodian receives only a limited, indivisible interest, the custodian cannot allot the land for exclusive use.
